newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan dollar volatility "normal" - central bank.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan dollar volatility "normal" - central bank.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank said on Friday the volatility that pushed the local currency sharply higher in recent days reflected normal trends both inside Taiwan's foreign exchange market and abroad.

"Movements in the foreign exchange market reflect international and domestic trends. Appreciation and depreciation are normal," central bank vice governor Liang Cheng-chin told reporters after the forex market close.

Liang would not be drawn when asked at an afternoon news conference whether the bank had intervened during a dramatic rise in the value of the Taiwan dollar during the past week, merely restating the bank's pro-market policy.
"The central bank's monetary policy remains to respect market functions," Liang said.
After rising through the week to a seven-month high close on Thursday of T$27.338 to the U.S. dollar, the local unit slipped slightly on Friday to end at T$27.391.
Turnover was an active US$435 million, compared with US$357 million.
In his comments, Liang did not stray from a position stated as recently as Wednesday that the market's sudden volatility after months of listless trade was both normal and beneficial.

Tuan Chin-sheng, deputy director general of the central bank's foreign exchange department, told reporters on Wednesday that the week's inward and outward remittances were normal and that the Taiwan dollar's movements were "helpful for increasing market activity and enlarging the market scale".
Dealers had been saying that the general upward trend was likely to continue ahead of the February 7 lunar new year holiday, traditionally a period of high currency demand.
But Friday's downturn prompted some dealers and analysts to say the appreciation may have run its course.
"Recent sharp movements in the exchange rate were mainly triggered by strong expectations the Taiwan dollar would go up," said one dealer at a foreign bank.
"Many investors took the chance to trade actively but they should trade more rationally next week," the dealer said.
Said a second dealer: "There are not too many fundamentals to cause the Taiwan dollar to rise sharply. Investors will soon realise that."
The central bank has consistently stood by what it calls a "stable to loose" monetary policy, hoping to accelerate what has been a disappointingly slow recovery without fanning inflation.
